title: Rankings and Reactivity: How Public Measures Recreate Social Worlds
extended_summary:
This article examines how public rankings become consequential social measures rather than neutral descriptors. The authors ask how quantitative rankings shape behavior, expectations, and institutional change, using U.S. News and World Report law school rankings as their case study. The central problem is reactivity: the process by which being measured changes what is measured.

The paper is not an intervention study or a coaching system evaluation; instead, it develops a conceptual framework for understanding how rankings produce effects. The authors analyze two mechanisms—self-fulfilling prophecy and commensuration—to explain how rankings alter decisions, redistribute resources, and change how actors interpret quality. They argue that rankings do not merely reflect social worlds but actively help recreate them by changing incentives, attention, and organizational identities.

The empirical context is U.S. legal education in the United States. The study draws on 136 open-ended interviews with law school administrators, faculty, and staff, plus additional interviews and document analysis, to trace how schools respond to rankings in admissions, budgeting, recruitment, marketing, and internal goal-setting. The main conclusion is that rankings have strong reactive effects: they can intensify stratification, encourage gaming and conformity to ranking criteria, and make quantitative measures more authoritative by embedding them in everyday institutional decisions.

identified_tools.name: CAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Computer-assisted or other quantified evaluation systems used to measure and rank institutions rather than an interactive AI tutoring product.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper analyzes U.S. News and World Report law school rankings as a public performance measure shaping institutional behavior; it does not study an AI coaching or generative AI tool.

quality_tier_rationale: This is a sociological article about rankings and reactivity, not an empirical evaluation of an AI educational tool. It contains qualitative case-study methods but no AI system intervention or learner/teacher outcome evaluation.
impact_tier_rationale: No AI tool is studied, and no instructional or coaching impact is reported. The paper’s relevance is conceptual for measurement and accountability, not evidence of AI coaching effectiveness.
